profile.summary: This was a public competition, hosted with Topcoder, on predicting what happens to mouse CD8 T cells in a tumour when a single gene is knocked out. The organisers generated an in vivo Perturb-seq data set of 73 gene knockouts in T cells transferred into a melanoma model, annotated each cell as one of five states, and asked teams to predict the five cell state proportions for held-out knockouts, to rank all expressed genes by two therapy-motivated objective functions, and to propose a new objective function. The top-ranked nominations were then knocked out in a second experiment, so submissions were scored against a prospective screen as well as held-out data. The record is useful to anyone comparing methods that predict perturbation effects on cell state composition rather than full expression profiles.

summary_quotes.text: We launched a world-wide computational challenge to predict the effects of gene perturbations and to devise objective functions for prioritizing gene perturbations that lead to desired T-cell state distributions.
We supported the challenge by generating a single-cell Perturb-seq dataset profiling the effect of knocking out 73 individual expert-defined genes in T cells transferred into a mouse melanoma model.
More than 1,000 participants from 87 countries, with backgrounds in mathematics, computer science, biology, and related fields, registered for the competition.
We annotated four T cell populations as progenitor, effector, terminal exhausted, and cycling

we selected the highest-ranked gene perturbations from the winning methods in Challenge 1 for experimental evaluation in Challenge 2. The experimental results were used to evaluate and rank all Challenge 2 submissions.

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The biological question is which gene knockout shifts tumour-infiltrating CD8 T cells away from terminal exhaustion and towards progenitor and other useful states, which matters for checkpoint blockade and CAR T therapies. The challenge turns that into three tasks. Challenge 1 measures accuracy: predict the five-dimensional vector of cell state proportions for knockouts that were measured but withheld. Challenge 2 measures usefulness for picking targets: predict proportions for every expressed gene, rank the untested genes by two objective functions, and be scored against a new experiment that knocked out the nominated genes. Challenge 3 measures the objective function itself: propose a score that ranks perturbations by how close they bring the cell state distribution to a desired one. The organisers point out that most existing benchmarks look like Challenge 1 alone, and that Challenge 2 tests the methods for biological efficacy.

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The training data come from an in vivo pooled CRISPR knockout screen. Naive CD8 T cells from OT-1 TCR transgenic mice were transduced with a guide library and adoptively transferred into congenic recipient mice, which were injected subcutaneously with B16-OVA melanoma cells one day after the transfer; the tumour-infiltrating T cells were collected 14 days later and sequenced. Screen 1 targeted 73 genes; after merging lanes it held 71,393 cells, and 31,009 remained after quality control for single-guide assignment and mitochondrial content. Leiden clustering gave five populations, annotated as progenitor, effector, terminal exhausted, cycling and other, and each perturbation is summarised by the proportions of those five states. A second experiment, Screen 2, targeted 59 genes, gave 75,227 cells and 25,738 after quality control, and served as the validation screen for Challenge 2. Perturbations with very few cells were dropped, with a cutoff of 32 cells for Screen 1 and 10 for Screen 2, leaving 59 perturbations for Screen 1 and 50 for Screen 2. A published screen of 180 transcription factors in the same mouse model was reannotated with the same five states and used as a third data set, with 173 perturbations after preprocessing. That screen activated the T cells before transfer and harvested them after 7 days rather than 14, and when the five cell states were mapped onto it some clusters could not be assigned. The two example objective functions were defined on the proportion vectors, with the unperturbed Screen 1 proportions as the reference point.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: In Challenge 1 a submission is a five-number proportion vector per held-out knockout. Seven knockouts were withheld; three of them, Aqr, Bach2 and Bhlhe40, formed a validation set with up to three submissions and feedback, and the final ranking used the average absolute error over the remaining four, with one final submission. The error is the sum of absolute differences across the five states, so lower is better. In Challenge 2 the predicted proportions for all untested genes are turned into two ranked lists with the ICB and CAR T objective functions. The top-ranked genes from the Challenge 1 winners were knocked out in Screen 2, the measured genes were ranked by the same objectives, and each submission was scored by an area under the curve comparing its predicted ranking with the measured one. That score lies between 0 and 1 and a random ranking is expected to give 0.5. Scores were computed on both the filtered and the unfiltered Screen 2, averaged within each, and the final score was the smaller of the two averages. Challenge 3 submissions were written reports, ranked by single-blind peer review among participants, averaged over reviewer ranks, then reviewed by the organisers. For the follow-up benchmarking of the top 20 methods, the organisers reimplemented them and used cross-fold validation instead of the seven held-out perturbations alone: perturbations were partitioned at random into 6 folds for Screen 1 and the public screen and 5 folds for Screen 2, each fold held out in turn, and the whole procedure repeated 5 times to give a standard deviation.

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The repository holds the organisers' own benchmarking code, not a submission server. Create the conda environment from environment.yml, get the split data files, and run the per-method scripts in the folder for the screen you want. The baseline script for Screen 1 loads a single AnnData file holding the internal splits, loops over six splits and five repeats for three predictors, nearest neighbour, kernel regression and bagged kernel regression, and prints the mean and standard deviation of the average error. Some data files are not in the repository and have to be downloaded from a Google Drive folder the README links.

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Challenge 1: the average absolute error, the sum of absolute differences between predicted and measured proportions across the five cell states, averaged over the held-out knockouts, lower is better.
